title: Familiarity Breeds Contagion ∗
venue: Journal of money credit and banking
abstract: Abstract Although the literature has studied the impact of social ties on credit markets, the possibility of social relations causing contagion remains unexplored. We study the Indian caste system and the group loan structure, where members screen and monitor each other. Using loan‐month level data provided by a nonbanking lender, we find that shocks take the form of a loan default contagion within local caste networks, plausibly due to preexisting economic linkages. Several robustness tests rule out delayed propagation of shocks being mischaracterized as a contagion. Thus, we highlight a dark side of social ties in credit markets.

summary.oneLiner: Loan defaults spread through local caste networks in India's group lending, suggesting social ties can transmit credit shocks, not just support borrowers.
summary.overview: This paper asks whether social ties can spread financial trouble, not just financial support, through credit markets. The authors study group loans in India, where borrowers from the same caste screen and monitor each other. Using loan-month data from a nonbanking lender, they find that defaults spread within local caste networks, a pattern they call contagion (one borrower's default leading to others' defaults). They suggest this is plausibly due to existing economic links between group members, and robustness tests indicate the result is not just delayed effects of a shock being mislabeled as contagion.
summary.question: Can social relationships cause loan default contagion in credit markets, and not only help screen and monitor borrowers?
summary.method: Analysis of loan-month level data, supported by several robustness tests to rule out delayed propagation of shocks being mistaken for contagion. The abstract does not describe the estimation technique in more detail.
summary.data: Loan-month level data provided by a nonbanking lender, in the context of group loans and the Indian caste system. Sample size and time period are not stated in the available text.
findings: Shocks take the form of a loan default contagion within local caste networks.
The contagion is plausibly due to preexisting economic linkages between network members.
Several robustness tests rule out delayed propagation of shocks being mischaracterized as contagion.
summary.whyItMatters: The authors highlight a dark side of social ties in credit markets: the same networks that help group lenders screen and monitor borrowers can also transmit defaults across members.
